title: What is CriptEnv?
text: CriptEnv is an open-source secrets management platform with a Zero-Knowledge architecture. An alternative to Doppler and Infisical, it lets developers and teams manage environment variables, API keys and sensitive credentials with end-to-end encryption.

title: What is CriptEnv?
text: All secrets are encrypted 100% client-side with AES-256-GCM. The server never receives plaintext data — even with full access to the database, it is impossible to decrypt your credentials.

title: Core Concepts
text: Core Concepts

title: Core Concepts
text: Understand how projects, environments, vaults and the remote CLI connect to protect secrets end to end.

title: Core Concepts
text: CriptEnv is zero-knowledge: secrets are encrypted on the client and the server stores only encrypted blobs.

title: Core Concepts
text: Zero-Knowledge All encryption happens on your device. The API never receives plaintext secrets or the project's Vault password. Projects Projects group related secrets and have their own Vault password to protect your data. Environments Environments separate configuration by stage, such as development, staging and production. The Pro and Max plans allow extra environments, which can be restricted to admins. Remote Vault The remote vault is the source of truth. It stores encrypted blobs and stays in sync across CLI, web and team. Vault Password Project password used only on the client to derive keys, decrypt in memory and prove vault access. Import/Export Push imports .env files into the remote vault. Pull exports remote secrets to local files.

title: Core Concepts
text: Zero-Knowledge — How does it work? The CLI reads the project Vault password via prompt or CRIPTENV_VAULT_PASSWORD. The environment key is derived locally with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 and HKDF. Secrets are encrypted or decrypted in memory with AES-256-GCM. The API receives only ciphertext, IV, auth tag, checksum and metadata.

title: Core Concepts
text: If the project's Vault password is lost, that project's encrypted secrets cannot be recovered by the server.

title: Core Concepts
text: Projects and Environments Projects are collaboration namespaces. Environments isolate values by stage without mixing production, staging and development.

title: Core Concepts
text: CLI as a Remote Terminal The CLI does not keep a local secrets vault as its main flow. It resolves project and environment through the API, downloads encrypted blobs, operates in memory and sends the new encrypted blobs back.

title: Core Concepts
text: Import and Export Use files when you need to migrate from an existing .env or materialize secrets for local execution: Files exported as .env contain plaintext. Add them to .gitignore and treat them as local secrets.

title: Vercel integration

title: Vercel integration

Connect the project In the CriptEnv dashboard, open Integrations, choose Vercel and paste the token and the project ID or name. Team projects also need the team ID (team_..., under Team Settings). Or use the CLI: Connect with the CLI Validate the connection Validation fetches the Vercel project with the stored token, so it catches a wrong token, project or team before the first sync.

title: Vercel integration
text: Vercel environments Every sync writes to one Vercel environment: production, preview or development. It defaults to the name of the CriptEnv environment; use --target when the names differ. Environment mapping

title: Vercel integration

title: Vercel integration

title: githubAction
text: Use CriptEnv's official Action (@criptenv/action) to decrypt and inject your environment variables straight into your GitHub Actions workflows.

title: githubAction
text: The CriptEnv GitHub Action needs a valid API token. You can create one in Dashboard → Tokens. It is a CI token (ci_...); to read a restricted environment, create the token for that environment.

title: githubAction
text: Setup Store the CI token and vault password in GitHub In the CriptEnv dashboard, create a CI token (starts with ci_) with the read:secrets scope. Because CriptEnv is zero-knowledge, the token alone only downloads encrypted values: to get plaintext values the Action also needs the project's vault password. Store both as Repository Secrets. Add secrets in GitHub Get the project ID Copy your project ID from the CriptEnv dashboard. The action needs it to know which project to decrypt. Add the Action to your workflow Configure your GitHub Actions workflow to run the CriptEnv action before your build or deploy commands.

title: githubAction
text: Inputs The Action accepts the following inputs: CriptEnv CI token (starts with ci_). Pass it through GitHub Secrets. Project ID in CriptEnv. Project vault password (via GitHub Secrets). With it, the Action exports plaintext values; without it, variables receive the ciphertext. Target environment (e.g. production, staging). Default: production. CriptEnv API URL. Default: https://criptenv-api.77mdevseven.tech/api/v1. Prefix for the environment variables. Default: SECRET_.

title: Security
text: Security

title: Security
text: CriptEnv is built on a zero-knowledge architecture, so your environment secrets are never exposed to the server. All encryption happens on the client: the server only stores encrypted data that cannot be decrypted without the project's vault password.

title: Security
text: The project vault password is never sent to the server. It is used locally to derive encryption keys that never leave your device.

title: Security
text: Security principles Confidentiality Every secret is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before it is stored or transmitted. The server never sees plaintext. Integrity AES-GCM provides built-in authentication (128-bit GCM auth tag), so any tampering with encrypted data is detected immediately on decryption. Environment isolation Each environment gets its own key, derived with HKDF from the vault key and the environment ID. A key from one environment cannot decrypt another environment's secrets. Restricting an environment is a different thing: an access rule enforced by the server. Since there is one vault password per project, the restriction stops the server from handing over the data, but does not take back what someone has already downloaded. Brute-force resistance Key derivation uses PBKDF2 with 100,000 HMAC-SHA256 iterations, making brute-force attacks computationally expensive even with specialized hardware.

title: Security
text: Key hierarchy CriptEnv uses a well-defined key hierarchy to isolate environments and projects: 100k iterations Vault key (256-bit) Environment key (256-bit) Encrypted secrets

title: Security
text: Security documentation Encryption protocol Technical details on algorithms, parameters and the full key-derivation flow. Zero-knowledge architecture How the zero-knowledge model protects your data, and what the server can and cannot see. Threat model Analysis of attack scenarios, risk levels and implemented mitigations.

title: Zero-Knowledge Architecture
text: Zero-Knowledge Architecture

title: Zero-Knowledge Architecture
text: CriptEnv's zero-knowledge architecture ensures the server never has access to your secret values in plaintext. All encryption and decryption happen exclusively on the user's client, using the project's vault password, which is never transmitted.

title: Zero-Knowledge Architecture
text: Put simply: even if the server were fully compromised, attackers would only get encrypted data, which is useless without the project's vault password.

title: Zero-Knowledge Architecture
text: What is zero knowledge? In CriptEnv, "zero knowledge" means the server can confirm you have the right password (through the vault proof) without ever learning that password or getting the keys derived from it. This differs from traditional systems where the server stores password hashes and the data: in CriptEnv, the encrypted values are useless even to whoever controls the server.

title: Zero-Knowledge Architecture
text: How client-side encryption works The whole encryption process runs in the browser with the Web Crypto API:

title: Zero-Knowledge Architecture
text:
What the server sees vs. doesn't see The server sees The server does NOT see ✓ Ciphertext (values encrypted with AES-256-GCM)
✓ Variable names (keys) — only values are encrypted
✓ IVs (initialization vectors — not secret)
✓ Auth tags (GCM authentication tags)
✓ PBKDF2 salts (random per project, public by design)
✓ bcrypt hash of the vault proof
✓ Environment and project IDs (non-secret metadata)
✓ Creation and modification timestamps
✓ Organizational structure (projects, environments) ✗ The project's vault password
✗ The derived vault key (PBKDF2 output)
✗ Environment keys (HKDF output)
✗ Environment variable values in plaintext
✗ Any ability to decrypt the values

title: Zero-Knowledge Architecture
text: The vault proof mechanism The vault proof lets the server check that the user knows the right password without the password or the encryption keys ever being transmitted. The proof is derived from the same vault password but with its own random salt (proof_salt), separate from the salt of the encryption key. So the proof cannot be used to derive the encryption key, and the server keeps only a bcrypt hash of it.

title: Zero-Knowledge Architecture
text: Practical implications Forgot the password? There is no recovery mechanism. Since the server never had your password or keys, the data cannot be recovered without them. This is a feature, not a bug: it ensures no one but you can read your secrets. Security for teams In shared setups, each member reaches only the projects they're authorized for, and decryption still happens on the client. Auditing The server can log access events (timestamps, IPs, environment IDs) without ever seeing the secret values. That enables security auditing without breaking the zero-knowledge architecture.

title: Encryption Protocol
text: Encryption

title: Encryption Protocol
text: Encryption Protocol

title: Encryption Protocol
text: CriptEnv uses a multi-layer key-derivation chain so that every environment has its own isolated encryption key. The whole process runs in the user's browser: the server never has the keys or the plaintext values.

title: Encryption Protocol
text: Key-derivation flow The full derivation follows these steps:

title: Encryption Protocol
text: Cryptographic parameters Algorithm Iterations Salt size Key size PBKDF2 (vault key derivation) HMAC-SHA256 — hash-based pseudorandom function 100,000 iterations — slows down brute-force attacks 32 bytes (256 bits) — generated randomly per project when the vault is created 32 bytes (256 bits) — output vault key HKDF (per-environment derivation) SHA-256 — underlying hash function 256-bit vault key derived with PBKDF2 Environment ID (UUID) — gives each environment a unique key "criptenv-vault-v1" — application context 32 bytes (256 bits) — output environment key AES-256-GCM (data encryption) AES-256-GCM — authenticated encryption in Galois/Counter Mode 32 bytes (256 bits) — environment key derived with HKDF 12 bytes (96 bits) — generated randomly for each encryption 16 bytes (128 bits) — authentication tag for integrity checks The IV (initialization vector) is generated randomly for every encryption. Never reuse an IV with the same key — that would break GCM's security.

title: Encryption Protocol
text: Vault proof derivation Besides the encryption key, CriptEnv derives a separate proof used to authorize vault writes in the API. It proves knowledge of the vault password without revealing the password or the encryption key.

title: Encryption Protocol
text: Local metadata vs. remote vault Local metadata Remote vault The CLI keeps local metadata in SQLite in the user's home directory: The CLI's main flow does not store secrets locally. Secrets live in the remote vault and are decrypted only in memory. The cloud vault stores only already-encrypted values:

title: Threat Model
text: Database compromise Ciphertext and variable names exposed; values unreadable without the vault password Mitigated Scenario: an attacker gets full access to the server database, including users, environments and stored secrets. Values stored only as AES-256-GCM ciphertext PBKDF2 salts and IVs are public by design Only a bcrypt hash of the vault proof is stored, never the password or keys Variable names (keys) are stored in plaintext — avoid putting secrets in names Result: the stolen values are useless without the vault password. The remaining attack is an offline brute force on that password, slowed down by PBKDF2 — which is why a strong password matters. Malicious administrator Can read metadata; could serve tampered web code to capture passwords Partially mitigated Scenario: a server administrator or insider with privileged access tries to read user data. Stored values cannot be decrypted with what the server holds The CLI encrypts locally and does not run code served by the web app The code is open source, so the client logic can be reviewed Result: an administrator sees metadata (timestamps, IDs, variable names) but not the values. As in any web-based zero-knowledge app, whoever controls the server could ship altered JavaScript that captures the password typed in the browser; users who need to rule this out should use the CLI. Man-in-the-middle (MITM) Traffic interception, but values travel already encrypted Mitigated Scenario: an attacker intercepts network traffic between the client and the server. TLS (HTTPS) for all communication HSTS to prevent downgrades to HTTP Values are encrypted before they are sent The vault password and derived keys never cross the network Result: even with TLS broken, the attacker would only see AES-256-GCM ciphertext. A broken TLS could still expose session tokens, metadata and the web app's code. XSS (cross-site scripting) Code running in the app could read data decrypted in memory Partially mitigated Scenario: an attacker injects scripts that run in the context of the user's browser. Restrictive Content Security Policy (CSP) React escapes rendered content by default HttpOnly cookies for session tokens Result: if an XSS succeeds despite these measures, the attacker could read secrets decrypted in memory and the vault password while it is typed during that session. Session hijacking API access as the user, but only to encrypted data Mitigated Scenario: an attacker steals the user's session token and impersonates them on the server. Sessions expire automatically Users can list and revoke their active sessions The vault password is not part of the session Result: the attacker can call the API, but the data returned is encrypted. Without the vault password, nothing can be decrypted — though metadata could be read and data deleted until the session is revoked. Brute force on the password Attempts to guess the vault password Depends on password strength Scenario: an attacker tries to guess the project's vault password by testing many combinations — online against the API, or offline with a stolen database. PBKDF2 with 100,000 iterations makes every attempt slow Random salt per project (prevents rainbow tables and attacking many vaults at once) Rate limiting on the API (online attempts only) AES-GCM auth tag makes a wrong password fail immediately Result: at ~100 ms per attempt on one CPU core, testing 1 billion passwords takes about 3 years — and GPUs run many attempts in parallel. Rate limiting does not help against an offline attack, so security rests on a long, random password.

title: Threat Model
text: Your responsibility: the system's security fundamentally depends on the strength of the vault password. Use a long, unique password generated by a password manager. The zero-knowledge architecture cannot protect a weak or reused password.

title: overview
text: Manage your secrets straight from the terminal — with end-to-end encryption and zero knowledge on the server side.

title: overview
text: Philosophy Terminal-first Every operation happens in your terminal. If you can open a shell, you can use CriptEnv. Zero-knowledge Your secret values are encrypted locally with AES-256-GCM before any sync. The server never sees them in plaintext. Remote vault The CLI works on the project's remote vault, keeping everything in sync with the web dashboard and the team.

title: overview
text: Features Secret management Store, rotate, import and export environment variables with strong encryption and versioning. Sync Push imports .env files into the remote vault; pull exports the remote vault to local files. Multiple environments Create and manage isolated environments (dev, staging, production) within one project. CI/CD Integrate with CI/CD pipelines. Log in headlessly, list secrets and deploy without exposing credentials. Integrations Connect cloud providers (Vercel, Render, Cloudflare Workers) and push or pull secrets. Rotation and expiration Set expiration alerts and rotate keys with automatic versioning.

title: CLI configuration
text: Learn how the CriptEnv CLI works as a remote terminal, what data stays local and how to use environment variables in automation.

title: CLI configuration
text: Remote terminal The main commands work directly on the project's remote vault. The CLI downloads encrypted blobs, decrypts them in memory when needed, re-encrypts in its own process and sends only ciphertext to the API. The backend never receives secret values in plaintext, and the project's vault password is never sent to the server.

title: CLI configuration
text: Local layout The ~/.criptenv/ directory holds only light metadata and local session credentials: File Description Local key used to protect CLI and CI session tokens. SQLite database with the session, current project, metadata cache and compatibility tables. The CLI's normal flow does not write a local copy of your secrets. Backups of ~/.criptenv/ still need protecting because they contain session credentials.

title: CLI configuration
text: Vault password The vault password belongs to the project. It derives the client-side encryption keys and is asked for only when a command needs to decrypt or change secrets. For automation, set CRIPTENV_VAULT_PASSWORD. The CLI uses it instead of the interactive prompt.

title: CLI configuration
text: Environment variables Variable Type API URL. Default: https://criptenv-api.77mdevseven.tech Default project for commands that accept --project. Project vault password for non-interactive use. API key (cek_...) that authenticates the process directly, with no login and no session written to disk — suited to CI, containers and read-only HOME directories. It is read only: to write or sync from a pipeline, use a CI token. Don't expose CRIPTENV_VAULT_PASSWORD in logs, shared shells or persistent histories. In CI, use the provider's secrets mechanism.

title: audit
text: Review the record of actions taken in the project. Audit logs track changes to the vault, secrets, environments, members, invitations, tokens, API keys and settings.

title: audit

Page (default: 1) Items per page (default: 50, max: 100) Filter by action, e.g. vault.pushed, secret.rotated, member.added, member.role_changed, invite.created, token.created, api_key.created Filter by resource type, e.g. vault, environment, member, invite, integration, ci_token, api_key, project

title: audit

Only an API key for every environment can have this scope: with environment_scope, creation returns 422 and reading returns 403. Events from restricted environments are shown only to the owner and admins, and never to an API key.

title: invites
text: Manage email invitations to add new members to a project. Invitations expire after 7 days and are tied to a specific role.

title: invites

title: invites

title: invites

title: invites

title: invites

title: ciTokens
text: Authentication tokens for CI/CD pipelines. They start with ci_, can be limited to scopes and to one environment, and the plaintext value is shown only once, at creation. In the pipeline, the token is exchanged for a 1-hour session (ci_s_…).

title: ciTokens
text: The token alone decrypts nothing: values are encrypted with the project's vault password. The pipeline needs the token and the vault password (for example, in the CRIPTENV_TOKEN and CRIPTENV_VAULT_PASSWORD secrets).

title: ciTokens

In practice, use the CLI (criptenv ci login) or the GitHub Action, which handle the exchange and decryption for you.

The restriction is enforced by the server and does not take back what someone has already downloaded.

title: vault
text: The vault stores and syncs each environment's encrypted secrets. Data always travels encrypted; the server never sees the values in plaintext (zero-knowledge).

title: vault
text: Zero-knowledge flow Before using these endpoints, understand the encryption flow. All encryption and decryption happen on the client:

title: vault
text: Reads accept a member session, an API key with read:secrets (restricted to its environment, if scoped) or a CI session. Writes require the admin role for people, or a CI session with the write:secrets scope; API keys are read-only here.

title: vault
text: Push secrets Sends the environment's encrypted blobs. The push replaces the whole set stored for the environment, so send every secret, not just the changed ones. Pass expected_version for optimistic concurrency control. Complete list of the environment's encrypted secrets Secret name (e.g. DATABASE_URL) — stored in plaintext AES-GCM IV (12 bytes, base64) Encrypted value (base64) AES-GCM auth tag (16 bytes, base64) Integrity checksum computed by the client Secret version (≥ 1) Proof of the vault password; required when the project has a vault configured Environment version you based the change on; omit to skip the conflict check Example — push secrets

title: vault
text: Conflict detection If the environment changed since expected_version, the API rejects the push with a conflict. A wrong vault proof returns 403. On a conflict, pull the latest version, reapply your change and push again.

title: vault
text: Pull secrets Returns every encrypted blob in the environment and its current version. Decrypt them on the client with the key derived from the vault password. Example — pull secrets

title: vault
text: Vault version Returns the environment's current vault version and blob count — a cheap way to check for changes without downloading the blobs. Example — check version

title: Authentication
text: Authentication

title: Authentication
text: The CriptEnv API supports several authentication methods for different scenarios: the web dashboard, third-party integrations and CI/CD pipelines.

title: Authentication
text: Overview Every authenticated request must carry a valid credential. The API tells the type apart by its format: Type Prefix Lifetime Use Session cookie 30 days, or 20 days without use Web dashboard and CLI (criptenv login) API key cek_ Until revoked or its optional expiration Containers and scripts, read only CI token ci_ → ci_s_ Token until revoked; each ci_s_ session lasts 1 hour CI/CD pipelines: reads, writes and syncs The hosting integration (Vercel, Render, Cloudflare) is not a credential: it is CriptEnv sending the variables of an environment to the provider. A restricted environment is reached only by the owner, the admins and CI tokens or API keys created for it.

title: Authentication
text: Session (cookies) When you sign in on the web dashboard, the server creates a secure HTTP-only cookie that the browser sends automatically on every following request. The CLI (criptenv login) gets a session of the same kind, with the same time limits, sent in the Authorization header and stored encrypted in ~/.criptenv. The session cookie is HttpOnly, Secure and uses SameSite=Lax. JavaScript cannot read it, which protects it against XSS. Login flow If the account has 2FA and the browser isn't remembered, sign-in returns a temporary challenge and creates no session cookie until the second factor is verified. Session expiration A session expires 30 days after sign-in, or earlier after 20 days without any request. It is not extended beyond 30 days; after that, sign in again.

title: Authentication
text: API keys API keys start with cek_ and last until revoked (or until their optional expiration). They suit server-to-server integrations that read projects, environments and encrypted vault blobs through the public API. Each key is bound to the project it was created in: GET /api/v1/projects lists only that project, and any other project answers 404, even one you are a member of. Scopes API keys only read. A key sits in a container or a file for months and works without a password or a second factor, so a leaked key must not change or delete anything. To write secrets or sync with hosting providers, use a CI token (short session) or the login. environment_scope must name an existing environment. A key acts as whoever created it: if that person loses access, so does the key. Scope Permission Read projects, environments and encrypted vault blobs Read the project's audit history. Only on a key without environment_scope Restricts the key to that environment. It is the only way for a key to reach a restricted environment Allows reads in every environment of the project, except the restricted ones Create an API key The key field is returned only on creation. Store it somewhere safe; if you lose it, revoke the key and create a new one. Use the API key in requests

title: Authentication
text: CI tokens CI tokens start with ci_ and are built for CI/CD pipelines. The pipeline exchanges the token for a temporary 1-hour ci_s_ session, with scopes such as read:secrets, write:secrets and write:integrations. Without environment_scope, the token covers every environment that is not restricted; a restricted environment needs a token created for it. Create a CI token Use a CI token in GitHub Actions Store the token (ci_...) and the vault password as GitHub Secrets. The Action exchanges the token for a ci_s_ session (POST /api/v1/auth/ci-login), downloads the blobs (GET /api/v1/ci/secrets) and decrypts locally with the vault password.

title: Authentication
text: CriptEnv supports social sign-in through OAuth 2.0 with these providers: GitHub — for developers who already live on GitHub. Google — quick sign-in with a work or personal Google account. Discord — for members of the CriptEnv community on Discord. The provider sends the user back to /api/auth/oauth/github/callback?code=…&state=…. The API checks the state, exchanges the code, creates or links the account, sets the session cookie and redirects to the app.

title: Authentication
text: Authentication errors Errors follow FastAPI's format: a detail field with a message, or an object with code and message for scope and environment errors.

title: Authentication
text: Best practices Use API keys for server-to-server integrations, with the minimum scopes needed. Use CI tokens in pipelines: each session lasts only 1 hour. Never expose API keys in frontend code or CI logs. Rotate API keys periodically and revoke unused ones. Set environment_scope to limit the impact of a leaked key.

title: overview
text: The CriptEnv REST API lets you bring secret management into any pipeline, tool or application. This reference covers the available endpoints, authentication, response format and error handling.

title: overview
text: Base URL Every API endpoint lives under this base URL: Authentication endpoints (sign-in, sessions, 2FA, OAuth) live under /api/auth instead. Every request must use HTTPS.

title: overview
text: Authentication The API accepts three kinds of credentials, each suited to a different scenario: Session HTTP-only cookie created at sign-in, for the web dashboard. Lasts 30 days, or 20 days without use. API key Token with the cek_ prefix for containers and scripts, read only. Can be restricted to one environment. CI token Token prefixed ci_ for CI/CD pipelines, exchanged for 1-hour ci_s_ sessions. For details on each method, see the authentication docs.

title: overview
text: Response format Every response is JSON, with Content-Type application/json. Success response List response Lists come wrapped in an object with the items and a total. Error response

title: overview
text: HTTP status codes Success — operation completed Created — resource created No content — operation with no body (e.g. DELETE) Bad request — invalid data or operation Unauthenticated — missing or invalid credential Forbidden — no permission for this operation Not found — resource doesn't exist or you can't access it Conflict — resource already exists or outdated version Unprocessable — request failed validation Too many requests — rate limit exceeded Internal error — unexpected server error

title: overview
text: Rate limiting The API rate-limits requests to protect the service from abuse. Limits depend on how you authenticate: Credential Limit Window per minute Public endpoints (per IP) API key (per key) CI token (per token) Auth endpoints (per IP) Rate limit headers are included in the responses: When the limit is exceeded, the API returns 429 Too Many Requests with a retry_after field (in seconds) in the response body.

title: overview
text: Pagination Most lists return every item at once. Paginated endpoints document their own parameters — for example, the audit log uses page and per_page (default 50, max 100).

title: overview
text: Reference by domain Authentication Sessions, API keys, CI tokens and OAuth. Projects Project CRUD and vault re-key. Environments Environments within a project. Vault Push, pull and versioning of encrypted secrets. Members Roles and project access. Invites Email invitations to join a project. CI tokens Tokens for CI/CD pipelines. Rotation Rotation, expiration and alerts. Integrations Sync with Vercel and Render. Audit The project's audit log. Health Availability checks.
